propositions.text: A man wearing a blue Halloween mask and holding a large knife robbed a variety store at night.
propositions.quote: A man wearing a blue Halloween mask and holding a large, butcher-style knife came into a variety store and demanded money from the woman working in the store that night.

propositions.text: The robber took money from the till and fled, actions caught on the store's security camera.
propositions.quote: When she opened the cash register, the robber scooped money from the till and ran out of the store. His actions were caught by the store’s security camera.

paragraphs.summary: A man in a blue Halloween mask robbed a store at night, taking money and fleeing, as caught on security camera, court states.

propositions.text: Police found a blue Halloween mask, large knife, and plastic cash register cover nearby the next morning.
propositions.quote: The next morning, police found a number of items in the neighbourhood: a blue Halloween mask, a large knife, and what turned out to be a plastic cover from the store’s cash register.

propositions.text: DNA on the blue mask matched only Marty David O’Brien with a probability of 1 in 33 billion.
propositions.quote: A test of the DNA found on the blue mask matched only one person: Marty David O’Brien. This match was characterized by the DNA expert in her report as follows: The estimated probability of selecting an unrelated individual at random from the Canadian Caucasian population . . . is 1 in 33 billion.

paragraphs.summary: Police found mask, knife, and cash register cover; DNA on mask matched only Marty David O’Brien with 1 in 33 billion probability, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. O’Brien was charged and convicted of three offences, including robbery.
propositions.quote: Mr. O’Brien was charged and convicted of three offences, including robbery.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. O’Brien was charged and convicted of three offences including robbery, court states.

propositions.text: At trial, nine witnesses testified before Justice Murphy without a jury.
propositions.quote: At a trial without a jury before Justice John D. Murphy, nine witnesses testified.

propositions.text: Investigating officer briefly referenced Mr. O’Brien’s prior criminal record and conduct during testimony.
propositions.quote: The investigating officer made brief references to Mr. O’Brien’s prior criminal record and conduct in the course of his testimony.

propositions.text: Defence did not object to this evidence nor request limiting it to narrative purpose.
propositions.quote: Not only was there no objection to this evidence by the defence nor any request that it be limited to a narrative purpose;

propositions.text: Defence used the prior record evidence in cross-examination of investigating officer.
propositions.quote: the defence used the evidence in its cross-examination of the investigating officer: Okay. Now in your testimony you briefly stated that you knew Mr. O’Brien to be known as an offender and that’s why you sort of steered in his direction in terms of this particular incident.

paragraphs.summary: At trial, nine witnesses testified; investigating officer referenced O’Brien’s prior record; defence did not object and used it in cross-examination, court states.

propositions.text: Only defence counsel referred to Mr. O’Brien’s reputation as a 'known offender' in closing submissions.
propositions.quote: Only defence counsel, in closing submissions, referred again to Mr. O’Brien’s reputation as a “known offender”.

propositions.text: Crown made no mention of character evidence in closing submissions; trial judge made no reference to it.
propositions.quote: The Crown made no mention of the character evidence in its closing submission and the trial judge made no reference of any kind to it.

paragraphs.summary: Defence alone mentioned O’Brien’s reputation in closing; Crown and trial judge made no reference to character evidence, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. O’Brien did not testify and defence called no evidence.
propositions.quote: Mr. O’Brien did not testify and the defence called no evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. O’Brien did not testify and defence called no evidence, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. O’Brien appealed on ground that verdict was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The basis of Mr. O’Brien’s appeal to the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal was that the verdict was unreasonable.

propositions.text: Court clerk asked counsel to address character evidence issue, though it was not raised in notice of appeal or factum.
propositions.quote: Before the hearing, the clerk of the court, at the panel’s request, wrote to counsel and asked that they be prepared to address the issue of character evidence. Mr. O’Brien had not raised this issue as a ground of appeal either in his notice of appeal or his factum.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. O’Brien appealed as unreasonable verdict; court clerk requested addressing character evidence though not raised by appellant, court states.

propositions.text: Crown acknowledged trial judge erred by not excluding or qualifying character evidence but argued error was not serious.
propositions.quote: At the appeal, the Crown acknowledged that it was an error for the trial judge not to exclude the character evidence or qualify its purpose, but submitted that since it was not a serious error, the curative proviso in s. 686(1) (b)(iii) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , should be applied.

paragraphs.summary: Crown acknowledged trial judge erred by admitting character evidence but argued error was not serious and curative proviso should apply, Crown argues.

propositions.text: All three judges found verdict not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: All three judges concluded that the verdict was not unreasonable.

propositions.text: Majority held trial judge made serious error allowing character evidence to be heard.
propositions.quote: The majority held, however, that the trial judge made a serious error in allowing the character evidence to be heard.

propositions.text: Trial judge made no reference to character evidence in reasons and did not disabuse himself from it or recognize it could not be considered.
propositions.quote: there was no indication that he “disabused himself from that evidence or was otherwise aware that it could not be considered” (2010 NSCA 61, 293 N.S.R. (2d) 78, at para. 94).

propositions.text: Crown failed to show judge was not influenced consciously or unconsciously by prejudicial evidence; curative proviso unavailable.
propositions.quote: The Crown had, as a result, not discharged its onus of demonstrating that the judge was not influenced, “consciously or unconsciously”, by the impugned prejudicial evidence (para. 95). The curative proviso was therefore not available.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed and new trial ordered.
propositions.quote: The appeal was allowed and a new trial ordered.

paragraphs.summary: Majority found serious error admitting character evidence, no proof judge was uninfluenced, curative proviso unavailable; appeal allowed and new trial ordered, court reports.

propositions.text: Dissenting judge would have dismissed appeal, finding error was not serious and caused no miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: The dissenting judge, Fichaud J.A., would have dismissed the appeal. In his view, the error in hearing the investigating officer’s propensity evidence was not a serious one and caused no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: Trial judge’s reasons affirmatively show improper evidence had no impact; judge relied entirely on DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge’s written reasons satisfy me affirmatively that the improper evidence had no impact. This, in my view, satisfies the Crown’s burden under the proviso. The judge’s words that he relied “entirely on the DNA evidence” to connect Mr. O’Brien to the robbery exclude any imputation to the judge of a veiled line of reasoning sourced in [the investigating officer’s] problematic testimony.

propositions.text: Dissent judge rejects idea of veiled reasoning from improper evidence coexisting with judge’s clear reliance on DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: Nothing in the decision suggests, even obliquely, that [the investigating officer’s] improper character testimony figured in the identification.

propositions.text: Curative proviso was available; dissent judge shares this view.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso was therefore available. I share this view.

paragraphs.summary: Dissenting judge would dismiss appeal, finding error harmless and judge relied entirely on DNA evidence; curative proviso available, court reports.

propositions.text: Whether trial judge’s error admitting bad character evidence and failure to address it was harmless or outside curative proviso.
propositions.quote: The issue before us was whether the trial judge’s error in hearing “bad character” evidence — and his related failure to specifically address that evidence in his reasons — was a harmless one, or whether it was outside the borders of the curative proviso.

paragraphs.summary: Issue is whether trial judge’s error admitting bad character evidence was harmless or outside curative proviso, court states.

propositions.text: At trial, only issue was identification; trial judge cautioned about such evidence.
propositions.quote: At trial, the only issue was identification. The trial judge cautioned himself about the need to approach such evidence with care, then concluded (2009 NSSC 194, 279 N.S.R. (2d) 157, at paras. 6-7):

propositions.text: Trial judge found strong circumstantial evidence linking blue mask to robbery beyond reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the circumstantial evidence is strong and sufficient to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that there is a connection between the blue mask and the robbery of the convenience store . . . on the previous evening.

propositions.text: Video shows blue mask and knife; cash register part found linked to store; evidence establishes mask associated with robbery beyond reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: Given the fact that the video clearly shows someone wearing a blue mask, or the blue and black mask, it clearly shows the use of a knife, and the evidence from the person who was in charge of the cash at the store, who returned to the store that night, clearly links the cash register part found to the cash register, because her notations and notations of others were on it. I am satisfied that the evidence establishes that the blue mask was associated with the robbery, and I am convinced of that beyond a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Investigating officer’s character evidence played no role in this finding.
propositions.quote: The investigating officer’s character evidence played no role in this finding.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found strong circumstantial evidence linking mask to robbery beyond reasonable doubt; character evidence played no role, court reports.

propositions.text: Trial judge said identification depended entirely on DNA evidence linking mask to accused beyond reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: The question then becomes whether the mask is connected to the accused, to Mr. O’Brien beyond a reasonable doubt, and that depends, as I have indicated, entirely on the DNA evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge said identification depended entirely on DNA evidence linking mask to accused beyond reasonable doubt, court reports.

propositions.text: Trial judge concluded DNA evidence clearly ties Mr. O’Brien to mask based on irrefutable match.
propositions.quote: After reviewing the DNA evidence for several paragraphs, the trial judge concluded that it “clearly ties” Mr. O’Brien to the mask, based on the irrefutable match between his DNA and the DNA found in the mask (para. 13).

propositions.text: DNA evidence establishes accused’s identity as robber beyond reasonable doubt, tying him to blue mask used in robbery.
propositions.quote: All this led the trial judge to conclude: . . . the DNA evidence establishes the accused’s identity as the robber beyond a reasonable doubt, ties him to the blue mask which was found, which I have indicated, based on circumstantial evidence, is clearly the mask that was used in the robbery.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge concluded DNA evidence clearly ties O’Brien to mask and establishes identity as robber beyond reasonable doubt, court reports.

propositions.text: Propensity evidence from investigating officer played no part in convictions; trial judge relied entirely on DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: The propensity evidence from the investigating officer clearly played no part in the convictions. As Fichaud J.A. noted, not only did the trial judge expressly state that he relied entirely on the DNA evidence to identify Mr. O’Brien, his detailed reasons confirm this exclusive reliance.

propositions.text: When trial judge expressly concludes independently of inadmissible evidence, no unfairness or miscarriage of justice arises.
propositions.quote: This evokes the words of McLachlin J. in R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393, at pp. 415-16, where she noted that when a trial judge expressly arrives at a conclusion on the critical issue “independently of the inadmissible evidence . . . no unfairness can be said to arise, nor has there been a miscarriage of justice” (see also R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86, [2001] 3 S.C.R. 823, at para. 30).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds propensity evidence played no part; trial judge relied entirely on DNA; cites precedent that independent conclusions avoid unfairness, court states.

propositions.text: Trial judge’s statement of relying entirely on DNA means he did not rely on character evidence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge said in his reasons that he relied “entirely” on the DNA evidence (para. 8). That meant that he did not rely on the character evidence.

propositions.text: Imputing reliance on character evidence despite judge’s contrary statement creates uncharted appellate review issues.
propositions.quote: Imputing such reliance into reasons that state the contrary creates a new, unchartable universe of appellate review where even if the reasons reveal a proper grasp of the facts and the law, the trial judge may nonetheless find the integrity of his or her decision undermined by the possibility that judicial silence on an issue will be interpreted as “unconscious” judicial error.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds trial judge’s statement means no reliance on character evidence; imputing otherwise creates uncharted appellate review issues, court states.

propositions.text: Trial judges must show how result was reached but need not itemize every issue or thought process.
propositions.quote: A trial judge has an obligation to demonstrate through his or her reasons how the result was arrived at. This does not create a requirement to itemize every conceivable issue, argument or thought process.

propositions.text: Trial judges’ reasons are reviewed based on what they say, not speculative imagination; judges not held to abstract perfection standard.
propositions.quote: Trial judges are entitled to have their reasons reviewed based on what they say, not on the speculative imagination of reviewing courts. As Binnie J. noted in R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 869, at para. 55, trial judges should not be held to some “abstract standard of perfection”.

paragraphs.summary: Court states trial judges must explain results but not every thought; reasons reviewed on their words, not speculation; cites precedent, court states.

propositions.text: Trial judge’s reasoning was impeccable with no suggestion of subconscious subversion of articulated thoughts.
propositions.quote: The trial judge was entitled to be taken at his word. His chain of fact, law and logic in this case was impeccable. I see nothing about his approach that suggests a subconscious subversion of his articulated thoughts.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds trial judge’s reasoning impeccable with no suggestion of subconscious error, court states.

propositions.text: Admission of improper character evidence was harmless error causing no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: I therefore agree with Fichaud J.A. that the admission of the improper character evidence was a harmless error of law that caused no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees admission of improper character evidence was harmless error causing no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice, court concludes.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed and convictions restored.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal and restore the convictions.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows appeal and restores convictions, court concludes.

propositions.text: The Crown invokes DNA evidence to salvage convictions from an unfair trial.
propositions.quote: the Crown invokes the magic of DNA evidence to salvage convictions obtained in what all the judges of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal agreed was an unfair trial.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent says the Crown uses DNA evidence to save convictions from an unfair trial.

propositions.text: Respondent was convicted as masked robber; only live issue was identification; DNA traces on masks found near crime scene linked him.
propositions.quote: The respondent was convicted as the “masked robber” of a convenience store in Amherst, Nova Scotia. The only live issue was identification. There was no evidence, circumstantial or otherwise, linking him to the crime except for traces of DNA on one of two masks later found abandoned near the scene of the crime.

propositions.text: Unfairness arose because police told court about respondent's reputation as habitual criminal unrelated to charged offences.
propositions.quote: The unfairness arose because the police, in the absence of such other evidence, decided to tell the court all about the respondent’s reputation as a habitual criminal in relation to other matters unconnected to the offences for which he was charged.

paragraphs.summary: The court states respondent was convicted based on DNA and unfairly linked to unrelated criminal reputation evidence.

propositions.text: Trial judge admitted propensity evidence without comment and did not recognize unfairness.
propositions.quote: The trial judge let in the propensity evidence without comment and gave no hint in his reasons that he recognized that the police branding of the respondent as a career criminal was against basic principles of trial fairness.

propositions.text: Trial judges may be presumed to know the law but sometimes misapply it, requiring appellate review.
propositions.quote: Trial judges may be presumed to know the law but occasionally they misapply it. Otherwise, there would be no need for appellate courts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge admitted improper evidence without recognizing unfairness, noting judges can err.

propositions.text: Respondent, sentenced to over six years, deserves assurance trial judge recognized propensity evidence danger; reasons do not provide it.
propositions.quote: The respondent, now sentenced to six years and six months in prison, is entitled to know that the trial judge recognized the danger of propensity evidence and consciously put it aside. The trial judge’s reasons provide no assurance on that point

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes respondent deserves assurance trial judge recognized propensity evidence danger, but reasons lack it.

propositions.text: Majority finds trial judge's 'entirely' reliance on DNA makes unfairness harmless, but court disagrees ignoring trial context.
propositions.quote: A majority of my colleagues conclude that the trial judge’s use of the word “entirely” in relation to his reliance on the DNA evidence is enough to render the unfairness of the trial harmless. To do so, in my view, ignores the context of the trial as a whole.

propositions.text: DNA reliability is established but handling errors cause wrongful convictions when no other evidence links accused to crime.
propositions.quote: The reliability of DNA science is well established, but problems in the handling of DNA samples and management of the test results have given rise to a number of wrongful convictions where (as here) there was not a shred of other probative evidence to connect an accused to the crime.

propositions.text: Curative proviso requires Crown to prove no substantial wrong or miscarriage despite unfair trial.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso in s. 686(1) (b)(iii) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , requires the Crown, not the defence, to show that despite the unfair trial, there was no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: Court does not believe Crown discharged onus; agrees with court below's caution; would dismiss appeal.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I do not believe that the Crown has discharged its onus. I agree with the caution exercised by the majority in the court below. I would dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with majority that DNA alone cures unfairness, finds Crown failed burden, and would dismiss appeal.

propositions.text: Crown evidence portrayed respondent as bad person likely to commit robbery; inadmissible evidence was extensive.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s evidence at trial sought to portray the respondent as a “bad person” of the sort likely to commit the robbery of a convenience store. Beveridge J.A. stated that “the inadmissible evidence was no mere inadvertent slip. It went on for some pages in the transcript.

propositions.text: Crown cannot prove case by showing accused's misconduct unrelated to charged offence to show propensity.
propositions.quote: It has been established for over 100 years that the Crown cannot make its case by showing that the accused engaged in misconduct other than that alleged against him for the purpose of showing that the accused was the type of person who would commit the crime alleged.

propositions.text: Police investigator testified respondent was involved in multiple incidents and was known as active criminal in area.
propositions.quote: So just at this particular time in 2004 in October there was . . . Marty O’Brien was thought to be involved in a number of incidences [sic] within Amherst and within the county . . . .

propositions.text: Officer testified respondent's criminal background was common knowledge in police detachment.
propositions.quote: I’ve known Marty O’Brien and he’s known me for years. I don’t know, maybe 10 or maybe 15, 20 years, and I know his . . . I don’t know everything he does, but I know his criminal background, and it was common knowledge within our office and within the RCMP detachment in Amherst that Marty O’Brien was an active criminal

propositions.text: Police said respondent denied involvement; later convicted and DNA order issued.
propositions.quote: So I went to the county jail, and I spoke to Marty O’Brien with regards to his being involved and he denied any involvement in it whatsoever. So I . . . after this, I checked . . . later on it became known that Marty O’Brien was convicted in court for a number of offences and a DNA order was issued to be taken on Marty O’Brien.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports earlier decision that Crown improperly introduced extensive bad character evidence from police testimony.

propositions.text: Defence counsel did not object; trial judge did not intervene or show concern about improper evidence.
propositions.quote: It is true that counsel for the defence did not object. Nor did the trial judge intervene or otherwise express any concern about (or even awareness of) the impropriety of the evidence.

propositions.text: Both majority and minority below found bad character evidence wholly inadmissible and trial unfair.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, both the majority and the minority in the court below found the evidence of bad character to be wholly inadmissible and the trial on that account to be unfair.

propositions.text: Prejudice from propensity evidence risks unfocused trial and wrongful conviction, undermining presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: It is frequently mentioned that “prejudice” in this context is not the risk of conviction. It is, more properly, the risk of an unfocussed trial and a wrongful conviction. The forbidden chain of reasoning is to infer guilt from general disposition or propensity.

propositions.text: Propensity evidence predisposes trier of fact to accept guilt more readily, undermining Charter rights.
propositions.quote: Propensity evidence is designed to predispose the trier of fact to accept more readily as credible the guilt of the accused than would otherwise be the case.

propositions.text: Use of propensity evidence in this case was not inadvertent slip but extensive.
propositions.quote: As mentioned, Beveridge J.A. noted that its use in this case “was no mere inadvertent slip” (para. 68).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes defence did not object but lower courts found bad character evidence inadmissible and trial unfair due to propensity evidence risks.

propositions.text: Identification rested on two strands: red car and DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: The identification of the respondent as the perpetrator rested on two strands of evidence. (1) The Red Car

paragraphs.summary: The court states identification evidence had two strands: red car and DNA.

propositions.text: Red car seen near mask location; respondent's ex-girlfriend owned red car he had access to but no direct link to crime date.
propositions.quote: At about the same time as the robbery, a red car was seen by a witness leaving the general area where the mask and other items were subsequently found. The respondent’s former girlfriend testified that she owned a red car to which, during the relationship, the respondent had “access”.

propositions.text: Witness could not identify car as same or close color; trial judge found red car evidence unhelpful.
propositions.quote: She did not say the relationship was continuing as of the date of the robbery or that he had continuing access. The witness was shown pictures of the former girlfriend’s car, but did not identify this car as the one she saw, or provide any identifying features about it except that the car she saw was red. She could not even say whether the car in the photo was the same or close to the same colour of red. The trial judge correctly concluded that the “red car” evidence was essentially unhelpful.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds red car evidence weak and unhelpful for identification.

propositions.text: Forensic expert found DNA on masks; one matched respondent; DNA match does not prove guilt alone.
propositions.quote: A forensic expert recovered DNA from the two abandoned face masks and testified that in the case of one of the masks, the DNA matched that of the respondent.

propositions.text: DNA evidence is like fingerprint evidence showing contact but not proving commission of offence without more.
propositions.quote: The Crown acknowledged that the DNA evidence in this case was the equivalent to that of a fingerprint in the sense that it established that at some point in time the respondent had handled or even worn the mask. It did not, without more, establish that the respondent was the masked robber on October 11, 2004.

paragraphs.summary: The court states DNA matched respondent but does not alone prove guilt, like fingerprint evidence.

propositions.text: Trial judge relied entirely on DNA to link respondent to mask used in robbery but inferential leap remains.
propositions.quote: The trial judge said that he relied “entirely” on the DNA evidence to link the respondent to the mask, which the trial judge concluded (on other evidence) was the mask used in the robbery.

propositions.text: DNA evidence alone does not bridge gap from contact to committing robbery without other information.
propositions.quote: DNA evidence alone does little to bridge this analytical gap — unless one was also given the information from Sgt. Blakeney that it is not just any random member of the community whose DNA has been found on the mask, but the DNA of a career criminal who was known to be implicated in a string of similar incidents in the same area around the same time.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge relied solely on DNA but DNA alone does not prove robbery without other info.

propositions.text: Section 686(1)(b)(iii) allows upholding conviction despite trial judge's legal error if no substantial wrong or miscarriage resulted.
propositions.quote: Section 686(1) (b)(iii) permits an appellate court to uphold a conviction despite error of law committed by the trial judge where that error has not led to a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: Error here was admission of evidence portraying respondent as career criminal likely to commit robbery.
propositions.quote: The error of law in this case was the admission of the evidence portraying the respondent as a career criminal — exactly the sort of person one might expect robbed this convenience store.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the legal error was admitting evidence portraying respondent as career criminal, but curative proviso may apply.

propositions.text: Curative proviso applies only if trial outcome would necessarily be same despite error; Crown bears onus.
propositions.quote: The “curative proviso” is to be applied only in those cases where the outcome of the trial, irrespective of the error, would necessarily have been the same (Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739). The onus of establishing that this high standard is met is on the Crown

paragraphs.summary: The court explains curative proviso applies only if outcome necessarily same despite error; Crown must prove this.

propositions.text: Curative proviso applies if Crown proves on balance of probabilities error was harmless or evidence so overwhelming conviction inevitable.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso may be applied, according to its modern interpretation, where the Crown can establish on a balance of probabilities that the legal error is harmless, in the sense that no prejudice has resulted, or that, despite any prejudice caused by the trial judge’s error of law, the evidence against the accused is so overwhelming that a trier of fact would inevitably convict

paragraphs.summary: The court states curative proviso applies if Crown proves error harmless or evidence overwhelming on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Trial judge's silence on inadmissible evidence and use of 'entirely' insufficient to show error harmless.
propositions.quote: In the application of the curative proviso on the facts of this case, I do not think that it is sufficient to rely on the trial judge’s silence on the issues of the inadmissible police evidence. Nor should the Court’s refusal of a new trial hang on the thread of the trial judge’s use of the word “entirely”

propositions.text: If trial judge intended to distance from propensity evidence, he would have said so explicitly.
propositions.quote: If he had intended by the word “entirely” to distance himself from the inadmissible propensity evidence, I expect he would have said so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge's silence and 'entirely' reliance on DNA insufficient to show error harmless.

propositions.text: Concern does not impute flawed reasoning by speculation but reflects Crown's burden to prove improper evidence harmless.
propositions.quote: My concern does not “impute” flawed reasoning to the trial judge on the basis of “speculative imagination” (reasons of Abella J., at paras. 16-17). Rather, it reflects the general principle that the Crown, not the defence, bears the burden of showing that the improper evidence was “harmless”.

propositions.text: Abella J.'s reasoning reverses Crown's burden of proof, which is improper.
propositions.quote: In my respectful view, Abella J.’s reasoning is tantamount to reversing the Crown’s burden of proof.

paragraphs.summary: The court states concern is about Crown's burden to prove harmlessness, criticizing Abella J. for reversing burden.

propositions.text: Respondent argues bad character evidence prejudiced trial judge to accept DNA evidence uncritically.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues that the evidence of bad character was prejudicial because it predisposed the trial judge to uncritical acceptance of the DNA evidence.

propositions.text: Respondent submits DNA evidence impact could be dangerously exaggerated by judicial knowledge of his proclivities.
propositions.quote: The submission on his behalf was that “[t]he impact of DNA evidence found on the Halloween mask could have been dangerously inadvertently exaggerated by the judicial knowledge of Mr. O’Brien’s ‘proclivities’”

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues bad character evidence prejudiced the judge to overvalue DNA evidence.

propositions.text: Crown says trial judge unaffected by bad character evidence because he did not mention it in reasons.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s response is that the trial judge was not affected by the evidence of bad character because he didn’t mention it in his reasons.

propositions.text: Court below noted trial judge gave no indication of awareness of problem during evidence or in reasons.
propositions.quote: However, as noted by Beveridge J.A., the trial judge gave no indication that he was even aware of the problem — either when the evidence was being adduced or in his reasons for judgment.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues trial judge unaffected by bad character evidence, but court below found no indication judge was aware of problem.

propositions.text: Majority in Court of Appeal declined curative proviso partly because no other evidence linked respondent to crime.
propositions.quote: In this case, the majority in the Court of Appeal declined to apply the curative proviso in part because there was no other evidence linking the respondent to the crime.

propositions.text: Fingerprint evidence connects accused to object but needs other evidence to link accused to crime at relevant time and place.
propositions.quote: Fingerprint evidence will almost always afford cogent evidence that the person whose fingerprint is left on the object touched that object. However, the ability of the fingerprint evidence to connect an accused to the crime charged will depend on whether there is other evidence capable of establishing that the accused touched the object at the relevant time and place so as to connect the accused to the crime.

propositions.text: Mars distinguished in Samuels where other evidence linked accused to crime.
propositions.quote: In R. v. Samuels, 2009 ONCA 719 (CanLII), by contrast, Mars was distinguished on the basis that there was “other evidence” linking the accused to the crime (para. 17).

paragraphs.summary: The court reports lower court majority declined curative proviso due to lack of other evidence linking accused to crime.

propositions.text: Court below noted Crown conceded DNA on mask alone does not establish culpability; DNA can be transferred and persist for years.
propositions.quote: In the court below, Beveridge J.A. noted: “The Crown here concedes that the fact DNA was found on the blue/black mask does not, on its own, establish the . . . culpability [of the accused]” (para. 24). The presence of the appellant’s DNA on the mask is equivalent to a fingerprint. The Crown’s expert testified that only small amounts of DNA are sufficient, and can be present for years. In addition, the thrust of the Crown’s expert evidence was that DNA can be transferred or deposited by handling.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports lower court found DNA evidence alone insufficient to establish guilt due to transfer and persistence issues.

propositions.text: I do not agree with Abella J. that admission of evidence blackening respondent's character was harmless.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with Abella J. that admission of the evidence blackening the character of the respondent was harmless.

propositions.text: Trial judge's failure to address problematic police evidence is a deficiency that cannot be excused by his use of 'entirely'.
propositions.quote: The failure of the trial judge’s reasons to address the problematic police evidence is a deficiency that cannot simply be brushed off by reference to his use of the word “entirely”.

propositions.text: Crown argues trial judges are presumed to know the law.
propositions.quote: The Crown argues that trial judges are presumed to know the law.

propositions.text: Argument excusing trial judges' deficiencies by presumption of knowing law was rejected in R. v. Sheppard and should be rejected here.
propositions.quote: the argument that important deficiencies in trial reasons can be excused on the basis that trial judges are presumed to know the law was rejected as a general one-size-fits-all excuse in R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 869, and should be rejected here as well.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with Abella J. that evidence admission was harmless, finds trial judge's failure to address police evidence problematic, rejects Crown's presumption argument based on Sheppard.

propositions.text: Crown invokes R. v. Leaney where inadmissible police opinion evidence was deemed surplusage and curative proviso applied.
propositions.quote: The Crown invokes R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393. In that case, inadmissible opinion evidence was received from police officers but the curative proviso was nevertheless applied, per McLachlin J., at p. 415

propositions.text: In Leaney, trial judge found police opinion evidence unnecessary and mere surplusage, not vitiating conclusion.
propositions.quote: Given the trial judge’s clear statement that he arrived at his conclusion as to identify independently of the evidence of the police officers, their evidence assumes the character of mere surplusage, which does not vitiate the judge’s conclusion that Leaney was one of persons shown on the video screen.

propositions.text: There is a significant difference between Leaney's tolerance of inadmissible opinion evidence and prejudicial bad character evidence here.
propositions.quote: there is a significant difference between appellate tolerance of inadmissible opinion evidence in circumstances where the trial judge found that the opinion evidence was unnecessary to enable him to appreciate what he could see with his own eyes on a video (and the inadmissible opinions thus characterized as “mere surplusage”) and prejudicial evidence of bad character.

propositions.text: In Leaney, the problem was source of testimony, here the content itself is objectionable.
propositions.quote: The content of the officers’ testimony in Leaney was itself unobjectionable. The problem was that it was not their place to utter it. Here, in contrast, it is the information itself, and not just its source, that is objectionable.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown relies on Leaney where inadmissible police opinion was surplusage; court finds Leaney differs as here the content itself is objectionable, not just source.

propositions.text: Crown should not benefit from curative proviso as trial judge showed no awareness of police testimony problem.
propositions.quote: the Crown should not have the benefit of the curative proviso because the trial judge’s reasons demonstrated no awareness of the problem of the police testimony.

propositions.text: In R. v. Rahm, trial judge understood bad character evidence inadmissible if character not in issue, so no miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: This was not a jury case. During the course of the trial, the trial judge made it clear that he understood that bad character was not admissible where character had not been placed in issue.

propositions.text: No such understanding evident in trial reasons here.
propositions.quote: No such understanding is evident in the trial reasons in this case.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no curative proviso benefit as trial judge unaware of police evidence problem; contrasts with Rahm where judge understood bad character inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Trial judge's error of law cannot be dismissed as harmless; respondent entitled to new trial unless harmlessness affirmatively found.
propositions.quote: I do not believe that the trial judge’s error of law can be dismissed as “harmless”, and, unless we can make an affirmative finding to that effect, the respondent is entitled to a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes trial judge's error is not harmless; respondent entitled to new trial absent affirmative harmlessness finding.

propositions.text: Curative proviso may apply if error not harmless but case against accused is overwhelming making guilty verdict inevitable.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso may also be applied when, despite an error of law that is not harmless, the case against an accused is so overwhelming that a guilty verdict would be the only reasonable outcome of a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: Court states curative proviso applies if error not harmless but case against accused is overwhelming making conviction inevitable.

propositions.text: In Court of Appeal, Crown did not argue case was so strong that conviction was inevitable; dissenting judge agreed.
propositions.quote: In the Court of Appeal, the Crown did not even argue that its case was so strong that a trier of fact would inevitably convict. Nor did the dissenting judge make any such suggestion.

propositions.text: These concessions were correct.
propositions.quote: In my view, these concessions were correct.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Crown and dissenting judge in Court of Appeal conceded case was not inevitably convicting; court agrees.

propositions.text: Denying new trial based on appellate conjecture of harmless error or overwhelming evidence is exceptional.
propositions.quote: It is an exceptional thing to deny an accused the new trial to which he is otherwise entitled because of an appellate court’s conjecture that the error was “harmless” or that any reasonable trier of fact, properly instructed, would simply find the evidence of guilt to be overwhelming.

paragraphs.summary: Court states denying new trial based on appellate conjecture of harmless error or overwhelming evidence is exceptional.

propositions.text: In Trochym, burden on Crown to invoke curative proviso is higher than proving beyond reasonable doubt at trial.
propositions.quote: the burden on the Crown seeking to invoke the curative proviso “is a substantially higher one than the requirement that the Crown prove its case ‘beyond a reasonable doubt’ at trial”.

propositions.text: Appellate standard requires evidence so overwhelming conviction is inevitable, higher than trial standard.
propositions.quote: The standard applied by an appellate court, namely that the evidence against an accused is so overwhelming that conviction is inevitable or would invariably result, is a substantially higher one than the requirement that the Crown prove its case “beyond a reasonable doubt” at trial.

propositions.text: Higher standard reflects difficulty for appellate court to retroactively assess effect of excluding evidence.
propositions.quote: This higher standard reflects the fact that it is difficult for an appellate court . . . to consider retroactively the effect that, for example, excluding certain evidence could reasonably have had on the outcome.

propositions.text: Crown cannot establish its case against respondent was overwhelming.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Crown cannot establish that its case against the respondent was “overwhelming”.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Trochym that curative proviso burden is higher than trial proof; finds Crown cannot show overwhelming case here.

propositions.text: I agree with majority below that curative proviso does not apply and would dismiss appeal.
propositions.quote: I agree with the majority opinion in the court below that the curative proviso has no application, and accordingly I would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed, Binnie and LeBel JJ. dissenting.
propositions.quote: Appeal allowed, Binnie and LeBel JJ. dissenting.

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellant and respondent named.
propositions.quote: Solicitor for the appellant: Public Prosecution Service of Nova Scotia, Halifax. Solicitor for the respondent: Nova Scotia Legal Aid, Amherst.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees with majority below that curative proviso does not apply, dismisses appeal; notes dissent and solicitors.
